native_fields.root_cause: Raffle.sol:544 (`sponsorAmount = grossPot - protocolFee`, with grossPot = unsettledPot at :539, credited at :554) pays the sponsor 95% of the whole pot, including entries the sponsor bought through any address. `buyEntries` (Raffle.sol:215-233) has no entry cap once `reserveEntries` is met and does not exclude the rebated party. Each sponsor-funded entry therefore costs the sponsor only 5% of ENTRY_PRICE but carries full weight in the uniform draw (Raffle.sol:518). This breaks DESIGN.md's uniform "one entry costs 1,000,000 units" for exactly one cohort. Earlier buyers cannot exit after the sponsor's late purchase: refunds open only at endTime+2d (Raffle.sol:286-287), and anyone, including the sponsor, can draw at endTime (Raffle.sol:242).
native_fields.internal_pre: The raffle resolves NftWon (totalEntries >= reserveEntries, Raffle.sol:521). The sponsor controls or colludes with sponsorRecipient, which is the default setup. The attack pays off whenever the NFT value V > 0.05 * organic entries N.
native_fields.external_pre: The sponsor has k USDC available from the last block before endTime until releaseSponsorProceeds, typically minutes: requestDraw at endTime, then 30 confirmations, then settle and release. 95% of it comes back. A flash loan does not work because entries lock funds across transactions.
native_fields.impact: The cohort of organic ticket holders who bought before the sale closed is left holding the loss.
native_fields.mitigation: Stop the sale at the reserve in buyEntries (`if (lastEntry > reserveEntries) revert ...`), so no sponsor-rebated entries can be minted after organic demand meets the reserve. A buyer blocklist on sponsor/sponsorRecipient alone is not enough, because purchases are permissionless (sybil). A sponsor fill of the gap below the reserve remains possible; it is tracked as a separate lead.

native_fields.smell: (Outside the DoS lens; passed on to the economic/cross-cohort lens.) Only totalEntries >= reserveEntries decides the outcome (Raffle.sol:521), and nothing excludes entries the sponsor paid for. NftWon pays grossPot - fee back to the sponsor (Raffle.sol:544). So buying whatever is missing from the reserve costs the sponsor only the 5% fee on those entries, and lets it flip a raffle that missed its reserve after seeing demand. Path: reserve 10,000; organic buyers hold 2,000 entries (2,000 USDC) one block before endTime. The honest outcome would be CashWon: winner 1,600, sponsor 300 + NFT, treasury 100. Instead the sponsor buys 8,000 entries from a fresh address. The callback gives NftWon; settlement pays the sponsor 9,500 (net +1,500 on an 8,000 outlay), and the sponsor's address holds 80% of entries for its own NFT. With an NFT value V = 3,000 USDC, organic buyers' expected value falls from 1,600 to 600 (-1,000), the sponsor's rises from 3,300 to 3,900 (+600), and the treasury's from 100 to 500 (+400). These sum to zero.
native_fields.unverified: This is not a DoS issue. It is unclear whether DESIGN.md means the reserve to protect only the sponsor, in which case a sponsor buying in is the same as having set a lower reserve. Addresses the sponsor controls cannot be identified on-chain, so any fix is at the design level.
native_fields.description: Buyers rely on the 80% cash payout when the reserve is missed, but the sponsor can cancel it at 5% cost by buying in at the last moment, after seeing demand.

native_fields.smell: The VRF wrapper can never change. RaffleFactory stores it as an immutable (RaffleFactory.sol:86), builds it into the single implementation (RaffleFactory.sol:89, inherited immutable i_vrfV2PlusWrapper), has no admin to repoint it, and createRaffle (RaffleFactory.sol:97-148) never checks that the wrapper still works. If the wrapper is disabled or unconfigured, getVrfRequestPrice and requestRandomnessPayInNative (Raffle.sol:249, 257) revert for every raffle. If the wrapper's subscription runs out of funds, a paid request is accepted but never fulfilled. After such an event, sponsors can still create raffles and buyers can still buy (Raffle.sol:209-237), but no raffle can ever resolve. Each one only moves to Refunding at endTime + 2d (Raffle.sol:286-287) or drawRequestedAt + 2d (Raffle.sol:290-291). Buyers' USDC and sponsors' NFTs are locked for up to 30d of sale + 2d (or + 4d). In the unfunded case, whoever requests the draw loses the native VRF fee.
native_fields.unverified: The wrapper implementation is not in node_modules; only VRFV2PlusWrapperConsumerBase.sol and IVRFV2PlusWrapper.sol are. The disabled and unfunded behaviour therefore comes from public Chainlink v2.5 semantics, not from source in the repo. No principal is lost because the refund path stays intact. DESIGN.md treats the wrapper as a trusted canonical dependency and rules out mutable configuration, so this is probably accepted design. The impact is limited to time-bounded locking.
native_fields.description: Because the wrapper is immutable and never checked, a deprecation on Chainlink's side puts every live and future raffle into a "lock, then refund" mode that only redeploying the factory can fix.

native_fields.smell: In the NftWon branch, the full sale price for the NFT, sponsorAmount = grossPot - protocolFee (95%), is credited to sponsorProceeds at settlement (Raffle.sol:544, :554). releaseSponsorProceeds (:375-380) pays it with no check of prizeClaimed or winnerRedeemed, so the USDC leg is never tied to the NFT leg (redeemWinningTicket :334-336). native_fields.unverified: Whether a prize that can refuse transferFrom(raffle, winner, id) after escrow is in the threat model. DESIGN.md says "arbitrary prize contracts ... are untrusted", but it also says "Sponsor and treasury can claim independently after settlement", and IRaffle.sol:14-15 says "Supported prizes are honest, standards-compliant ERC-721s". Against a fully malicious prize, coupling alone would not protect buyers either, because the contract could fake delivery. The defect bites hardest for collections that are honest but can restrict transfers (pause, creator transfer-approval hooks, transfer-validator level changes, migrations) and for owner-upgradeable prize contracts.
native_fields.description: Concrete path. (1) Sponsor creates a raffle (reserveEntries = 1,000) whose prize is an owner-upgradeable ERC-721 that passes F:154-179 and the escrow checks at F:128-134. (2) Buyers buy 5,000 entries, so USDC held is 5,000e6. (3) VRF resolves to NftWon. (4) Sponsor upgrades the prize so transfers out of the raffle revert. (5) Anyone calls settleWinningTicket(w): sponsorProceeds = 4,750e6 and protocolFees = 250e6. (6) releaseSponsorProceeds sends 4,750 USDC to sponsorRecipient. (7) redeemWinningTicket(w) reverts at :334 forever. USDC is conserved (5,000 in = 4,750 + 250 out), but the winning-ticket holder is left holding the loss: no NFT and no USDC claim. With an upgradeable prize the sponsor can also recover the NFT. Minimal mitigation if in scope: in releaseSponsorProceeds, require prizeClaimed when status == NftWon. Trade-off: a winner who never redeems then also defers the sponsor's proceeds.

native_fields.smell: In the NftWon branch, Raffle.sol:544 (`sponsorAmount = grossPot - protocolFee`) and :554-555 make 95% of the pot payable to sponsorRecipient and 5% to the treasury. Neither depends on the NFT being delivered. `releaseSponsorProceeds` (:375-382) has no `prizeClaimed`/delivery gate. The only way the NFT leaves is `redeemWinningTicket` (:334-337). It reverts entirely if the prize contract refuses `transferFrom(raffle, ...)` or misreports `ownerOf`. No state converts an undeliverable NftWon prize into cash or refunds: NftWon can never reach Refunding, and `releaseSponsorPrize` is barred in NftWon (:397). The escrow proof at creation also comes from the same untrusted contract: the prize contract can call `onERC721Received` (:421-428) directly, and the factory trusts its `ownerOf` (F:128-132). native_fields.external_pre: After escrow, the prize ERC-721 refuses or redirects the clone's transfer of the prize. Possible causes: the collection admin pauses transfers, applies a transfer restriction (operator, owner-initiated or account freeze that hits the clone), or upgrades the collection. A third possibility is a sponsor-controlled collection whose admin seizes or locks the token. DESIGN.md: "arbitrary prize contracts ... are untrusted". The pause and transfer-restriction behaviours are general ERC-721 ecosystem facts, not code vendored in this repo.
native_fields.impact: The winning-ticket holder bears the whole loss. That is Alice, or anyone who bought the winning ticket on the secondary market at roughly the NFT's value. The NFT she won can never be delivered, and NftWon is terminal with no refund or cash fallback. Meanwhile 100% of the buyers' 12,000 USDC has already gone out: 11,400 to the sponsor recipient and 600 to the treasury. In the seize variant, where S controls the prize contract, S keeps both the NFT and the 11,400 USDC. This breaks money-map invariants 7 (the prize leaves exactly once, to the winner in NftWon) and 15 (every claimant can eventually collect). Suggested severity: Medium, because it depends on an external pre-condition on the prize contract.
native_fields.mitigation: In releaseSponsorProceeds(), and likewise in releaseProtocolFees(), add `if (status == Status.NftWon && !prizeClaimed) revert PrizeNotDelivered();` so the NftWon allocation is paid only against actual delivery. native_fields.root_cause: Raffle.sol:376. `releaseSponsorProceeds` pays out `sponsorProceeds` with no check on `status` or `prizeClaimed`. In `NftWon`, `_settleWinningTicket` allocates 95% to the sponsor and 5% to the treasury (Raffle.sol:543-544, 554-555) through permissionless, storage-only settlement. Neither step depends on the NFT leg in `redeemWinningTicket` (Raffle.sol:329-337) ever succeeding. `NftWon` also has no fallback for the winner: `enableRefunds` only accepts Active or Drawing (Raffle.sol:279-293), `releaseSponsorPrize` excludes NftWon (Raffle.sol:397), and `winnerProceeds` stays 0. The code assumes the escrowed ERC-721 can still be transferred out of the clone when the winner redeems. Real ERC-721s let an admin revoke that after deposit: OpenZeppelin `ERC721Pausable` (`_update` is `whenNotPaused` and reverts `EnforcedPause()`), Manifold Creator Core's admin-set transfer-approval hook (`setApproveTransfer`), Limit Break ERC721-C transfer validators (creator-set soulbound or OTC-blocking policies, account freezing), and upgradeable ERC-721 proxies. DESIGN.md says "arbitrary prize contracts ... are untrusted", but IRaffle.sol:14-15 assumes "honest" prizes. The code follows the weaker of the two.
native_fields.internal_pre: The reserve is met, so the result is `NftWon`. No other state is needed.
native_fields.external_pre: The prize collection has an owner-controlled transfer gate (pause, approve-transfer hook, validator policy or freeze, or proxy upgrade), and the sponsor controls it or colludes with whoever does. The common case qualifies: an artist raffling a token from their own Manifold or OpenZeppelin collection.
native_fields.impact: The buyer cohort paid 20,000 USDC. S takes 19,000 USDC and the treasury 1,000 USDC, and the NFT is never delivered. Winner W is left holding the loss: the claim on C#7 can never be redeemed and there is no cash or refund substitute. This defeats the protocol's trust-minimising guarantee ("Exactly one ERC721 prize is escrowed atomically at creation") while fully protecting the sponsor's 95%. S's cost is a token S controls anyway.
native_fields.mitigation: In `releaseSponsorProceeds` (Raffle.sol:375-376), add `if (status == Status.NftWon && !prizeClaimed) revert` so NftWon sponsor proceeds unlock only after `redeemWinningTicket` has delivered and verified the prize. Optionally apply the same gate to `releaseProtocolFees`. This narrows DESIGN.md's "claim independently after settlement" for the NftWon branch only. That is the branch where the sponsor can control the opposite leg, and the gate removes the sponsor's profit from blocking the prize.

native_fields.smell: DESIGN.md requires "Never move assets between raffle clones." `sponsorRecipient` is screened only at creation: `RaffleFactory._validateCreateParams` checks the `isRaffle` mapping (RaffleFactory.sol:163-169), and `Raffle.initialize` calls `_isProtocolDestination` (Raffle.sol:193), which skips the `isRaffle` query for addresses with no code (:602). Clones are deployed with CREATE (OZ `Clones.clone`: `create(value, 0x09, 0x37)`), so each future raffle address depends only on the factory address and nonce. These addresses can be predicted, and anyone can advance the nonce through the permissionless `createRaffle`. A sponsorRecipient equal to a future clone address therefore passes both screens. After a later `createRaffle` registers a raffle at that address, `releaseSponsorPrize` (:402-405) transfers the prize NFT into that clone without a delivery-time screen, and no function can ever move it out. The USDC path for the same recipient, `_transferQuote`, re-screens at payout (:565) and reverts, which strands `sponsorProceeds` instead. The same skip for code-less addresses in `_update` (:498 → :602) lets a ticket be sent to a future clone address, where it later becomes unreachable.
native_fields.unverified: No actor other than the sponsor (for sponsorRecipient) or the ticket owner or operator (for tickets) chooses these destinations. Pointing at the raffle's own address is caught (:599, `destination == address(this)`), and a recipient that is already a raffle is caught (RaffleFactory.sol:166; Raffle.sol:602-603). On current evidence this harms only the party who chose the address, so it is not reportable as a finding. It is listed because it is the one reachable state that violates DESIGN.md's cross-clone invariant, and because sibling payout sites screen inconsistently.

So the input that decides who gets paid, ticket ownership, can change after the VRF request. The calldata of the coordinator's fulfillment fixes randomWords[0]. Anyone watching the mempool can therefore compute winningEntry = randomWords[0] % totalEntries + 1 (Raffle.sol:518) and the ticket that contains it before the callback lands. They can then trade ahead of it: buy the winning ticket from an open listing, or sell known losing tickets into open collection offers. Path: a CashWon raffle with 1,000 entries and a 1,000 USDC pot. Holder H has an open listing for ticket #7 (entries 101-110) at 9 USDC. The fulfillment transaction is pending, and its random word maps to entry 105. A bot fills H's listing at 9 USDC before the callback, then calls redeemWinningTicket(7) after resolution and receives 800 USDC (Raffle.sol:339-342). H gives up about 791 USDC of value.
native_fields.unverified: I could not confirm offline whether Ethereum-mainnet VRF fulfillments go through the public mempool. Even if they do not, a back-run right after resolution sniping a stale listing causes the same loss to the seller. That makes the protocol's share of the blame small and mostly a question of listing hygiene. Chainlink advises against accepting inputs after a randomness request. The smallest change would be for _update to reject ticket transfers that are neither mints nor burns while status == Drawing, but that removes only the pre-resolution window.
native_fields.description: Because tickets remain transferable during Drawing, anyone who reads the pending fulfillment can trade against counterparties who cannot see it.

native_fields.smell: The NftWon/CashWon regime check (Raffle.sol:521) counts sponsor-bought entries, which are rebated 95% through sponsorProceeds (Raffle.sol:544). When organic demand N < reserve R, the sponsor can fill R-N in the last block before endTime at a 5% cost. That turns a CashWon raffle (buyers' EV 0.8 USDC per entry) into NftWon. Example with R = 1,000, N = 900, NFT worth V = 500 USDC: honest CashWon gives buyers 720 USDC EV and the sponsor 135 USDC + the NFT (635). If the sponsor buys 100 entries, the raffle becomes NftWon: sponsor = 950 - 100 + 0.1*500 = 900 (+265); buyers' EV = 0.9*500 = 450 (-270); treasury +5.
native_fields.unverified: (1) Whether under-reserve buyers are entitled to expect CashWon. The reserve may be meant only as sponsor protection, and organic demand reaching R gives the same regime. (2) The flip pays only when V is below roughly 0.8*R (an overpriced reserve); with V = 900 in the example it is unprofitable and helps buyers. (3) There is no sybil-proof code fix: the sale cap proposed for the dilution FINDING does not close this gap.
native_fields.description: A sponsor-funded fill of the gap below the reserve in the last block lets the sponsor choose the payout regime after seeing demand, at a 5% cost, and moves EV from under-reserve buyers to the sponsor.

native_fields.smell: The outcome predicate `totalEntries >= reserveEntries` (Raffle.sol:521) counts the sponsor's own entries. In NftWon the sponsor gets back 95% of whatever it paid in (Raffle.sol:544). So the sponsor can meet its own reserve at about 5% cost and turn a CashWon (80% of the pot to a buyer) into an NftWon whenever the NFT is worth less than the cash prize. Worked example (arithmetic checked): reserve 1,000; buyers hold 900 entries; the NFT is worth 500 USDC. If the sponsor buys 100 entries before endTime, the sponsor's expected value rises by 265 USDC, the buyers' falls by 270 USDC and the treasury gains 5.
native_fields.unverified: Whether this is an accepted mechanism-design property. The reserve is public, any party can push the total over it, and the sponsor can buy from fresh addresses, so there is no on-chain fix.
native_fields.description: Buying the reserve shortfall with the sponsor's own money lets the sponsor pick the outcome branch that is worse for buyers. This is probably accepted design and is reported only for calibration.

native_fields.smell: The outcome test `totalEntries >= reserveEntries` (Raffle.sol:521) also counts entries the sponsor paid for. In NftWon, 95% of every entry, including the sponsor's own, returns to sponsorRecipient (Raffle.sol:544, :554). So the sponsor can flip a raffle that is below reserve from CashWon to NftWon for a 5% toll on the gap. Example: reserve 10,000 entries, 8,000 entries bought by other users. The sponsor buys 2,000 entries at endTime-1, which Raffle.sol:216 allows. Without the flip (CashWon), the winner gets 6,400 USDC and sponsorRecipient gets 1,200 USDC plus the NFT back. With the flip (NftWon), sponsorRecipient gets 9,500 USDC (net +7,500 after the 2,000 USDC outlay) and the sponsor's tickets have a 20% chance of winning the NFT. With the NFT worth 5,000 USDC: sponsor expected value rises from 6,200 to 8,500 (+2,300). The other buyers' expected value falls from 6,400 to 4,000 (-2,400). The treasury gains 100. The changes sum to zero.
native_fields.unverified: This is outside Lens 6 (economic/MEV). DESIGN.md does not forbid sponsor participation, and any address can buy (Sybil), so this may be an accepted property of reserve auctions. The flip only pays when the sponsor values the NFT below 0.8 x the pot from other buyers (here, below 7,875 USDC). Buyers can see totalEntries and reserveEntries on-chain, but they cannot exit before the outcome except by selling the ticket, because refundTickets requires Refunding.
native_fields.description: The sponsor can meet the reserve with their own entries, 95% of which come back to them, turning a cash raffle into an NFT raffle after buyers have committed.

native_fields.smell: The result is a pure function of the single VRF word: `winningEntry = word % totalEntries + 1` and NftWon/CashWon (Raffle.sol:518-521). Every ticket range is public (`ticketRange` :451-455). Tickets stay transferable while Drawing and after resolution: `_update` (:497-502) only screens destinations, and the NatSpec at :491 says tickets are transferable "in every lifecycle state". Once the oracle's fulfillment transaction, which carries the proof, is visible and before `RaffleResolved` is mined, a watcher can derive the winning ticket ID. The watcher can then fill any resting marketplace order selling that ticket, or sell known-losing tickets into resting bids, before holders can see the result on-chain. Ticket holders with resting orders lose through adverse selection.
native_fields.unverified: (a) Whether Chainlink's Ethereum VRF nodes broadcast fulfillments through the public mempool or privately. (b) Whether the v2.5 coordinator's `fulfillRandomWords` accepts an observed proof from any caller, which would let a sniper deliver it and trade in one atomic transaction. The coordinator and wrapper sources are not vendored under packages/contracts. (c) Whether this goes beyond generic stale-order NFT MEV, given that the design deliberately keeps tickets transferable. The outcome cannot be re-rolled, because reverting a delivery does not change the proof. This is information leakage only; no protocol-held funds are at risk.
native_fields.description: Information about the winner leaks before the state change while the tickets it prices are still tradable. Blocking ticket transfers while `status == Drawing` would close only the pre-inclusion window and conflicts with the bearer-claim design.
